title: Valid time vs transaction time
description: Bitemporal modeling tracks two clocks: valid time (when the fact was true in the world) and transaction time (when the database learned it). A correction to last month's record keeps both — the old belief with its transaction interval closed, the new belief open. Without both, 'what did we know on March 1st' is unanswerable.
mechanism: Each row carries (valid_from, valid_to, txn_from, txn_to). Updates close the current row's txn_to and insert a new row. As-of queries filter txn interval contains T and valid interval contains T.
algo: As-of query adds two range predicates; indexed on (txn_from, txn_to) it stays O(log n + matches). Storage grows with correction count, not data size.
demo:
# rows: (value, valid_from, valid_to, txn_from, txn_to); None = open
rows = [
    ('price=10', '2024-01-01', '2024-12-31', '2024-01-05', '2024-03-10'),
    ('price=12', '2024-01-01', '2024-12-31', '2024-03-10', None),  # correction
]

def as_of(valid_t, txn_t):
    return [v for v, vf, vt, tf, tt in rows
            if vf <= valid_t <= vt and tf <= txn_t and (tt is None or txn_t < tt)]

print('known on 2024-02-01:', as_of('2024-02-15', '2024-02-01'))
print('known on 2024-04-01:', as_of('2024-02-15', '2024-04-01'), '(correction visible)')

title: Time-partitioned indexes
description: Time-partitioned indexes split data by time bucket — one index per day, hour, or month — so retention is a directory delete and recent queries touch only hot partitions. Each partition is an independent index with its own segments; a query over a time range opens exactly the partitions it overlaps. It is the standard layout for logs, metrics, and event archives.
mechanism: Route each document to the partition for its timestamp bucket. Maintain a partition manifest (bucket -> index handle). Query planner prunes partitions outside the time predicate before opening anything.
algo: Partition pruning is O(partitions) manifest scan. Retention delete is O(1) per expired partition — no tombstones, no merge.
demo:
# one index per day; queries open only overlapping partitions
partitions = {'2024-05-01': ['e1', 'e2'], '2024-05-02': ['e3'], '2024-05-03': ['e4', 'e5']}

def query(start, end):
    touched, out = [], []
    for day in sorted(partitions):
        if start <= day <= end:
            touched.append(day)
            out.extend(partitions[day])
    return touched, out

touched, rows = query('2024-05-02', '2024-05-03')
print('partitions opened:', touched, '(2024-05-01 pruned without I/O)')
print('rows:', rows)
# retention: drop a whole partition
del partitions['2024-05-01']
print('retention: dropped 2024-05-01 in O(1), remaining:', sorted(partitions))

title: TTL indexes
description: TTL indexes auto-delete documents after a time-to-live, using the document's own timestamp field. A background sweeper scans for expired entries and removes them in batches. They are the fire-and-forget retention mechanism for sessions, tokens, and ephemeral events — set the expiry at write time and never think about it again.
mechanism: Index the expiry timestamp; the sweeper periodically queries expiry < now (limit N per pass) and deletes matches. Clock skew across writers is the main correctness caveat — use server-assigned timestamps when ordering matters.
algo: Sweep is O(expired) per pass. Write is O(1) extra for the expiry field. Expiry precision is ~sweep interval.
demo:
import time

docs = []
NOW = [1000.0]

def insert(doc, ttl_s):
    docs.append({'doc': doc, 'expires': NOW[0] + ttl_s})

def sweep():
    expired = [d for d in docs if d['expires'] <= NOW[0]]
    for d in expired:
        docs.remove(d)
    return len(expired)

insert('session-abc', ttl_s=60)
insert('session-old', ttl_s=60)
NOW[0] += 61  # time passes...
print('sweeper removed:', sweep(), 'doc(s)')
print('remaining:', [d['doc'] for d in docs] or 'none (all expired)')

title: Event sourcing
description: Event sourcing stores the history of changes as an append-only event log instead of the current state — state is a fold over events. Time-travel is free (replay to any point), auditing is complete, and new projections are built by replaying. The cost is replay time, handled with snapshots every N events so restores start from a recent checkpoint, not from genesis.
mechanism: Append events (id, seq, type, payload, timestamp). Snapshot state every K events. Rebuild: load latest snapshot, replay events after it. Projections subscribe to the log and maintain their own views.
algo: Replay is O(events since snapshot). Snapshot every K events bounds restore to O(K). Append is O(1).
demo:
events = []

def append(etype, payload, ts):
    events.append({'seq': len(events), 'type': etype, 'payload': payload, 'ts': ts})

append('deposit', 100, 1); append('withdraw', 30, 2); append('deposit', 50, 3)

def replay(until_ts):
    bal = 0
    for e in events:
        if e['ts'] > until_ts:
            break
        bal += e['payload'] if e['type'] == 'deposit' else -e['payload']
    return bal

print('balance at t=2:', replay(2), '(time-travel: replay to any point)')
print('balance at t=3:', replay(3))
print('event log is the source of truth; state is derived')

title: Windowed queries
description: Windowed queries aggregate over sliding or tumbling time windows — 'error rate per 5 minutes over the last hour'. Tumbling windows partition time into fixed buckets; sliding windows overlap and update continuously. Stream processors assign each event to windows by event time (not arrival time), so late data still lands in the right bucket.
mechanism: Tumbling: window = floor(ts / size). Sliding: emit for every window of length L sliding by S containing ts. Watermarks track event-time progress; windows fire when the watermark passes their end.
algo: Assignment is O(1) per event. Sliding windows multiply state by L/S windows per event.
complexity: O(1) tumbling; O(L/S) sliding per event

title: Retention policies
description: Retention policies declare how long each data class lives — raw events 30 days, hourly rollups 1 year, daily rollups forever. Enforcement is tiered: hot partitions age to warm storage, then to cold object storage, then deletion. The policy is data, not code: changing '30 days' to '90 days' is a config edit, and the enforcer applies it on the next pass.
mechanism: Policy table: (data class, hot_days, warm_days, delete_after). Enforcer scans partition manifests, moves or drops partitions crossing thresholds. Legal holds override deletion per partition.
algo: Enforcement is O(partitions) manifest scan per pass. Tier moves are O(partition size) copies; deletes are O(1) metadata ops.
demo:
POLICY = {'raw': 30, 'hourly': 365, 'daily': None}  # days; None = forever
partitions = [
    ('raw/2024-01-01', 'raw', 400), ('raw/2024-04-15', 'raw', 40),
    ('hourly/2024-01-01', 'hourly', 400), ('daily/2020-01-01', 'daily', 2000),
]
NOW_AGE = 500  # pretend today is 500 days after the oldest
for name, cls, age in partitions:
    limit = POLICY[cls]
    action = 'DELETE' if limit and age > limit else 'keep'
    print('%-18s age=%4d limit=%-4s -> %s' % (name, age, limit, action))

title: Downsampling
description: Downsampling keeps history affordable: raw per-second metrics age into per-minute averages, then per-hour, then per-day. Each rollup level is computed once from the level below and the raw data is dropped per the retention policy. Queries automatically pick the coarsest level that satisfies the requested resolution — a year-long dashboard reads daily points, not 31 million raw ones.
mechanism: Rollup jobs aggregate (avg/min/max/sum/count) over fixed buckets into the next level down. Query planner maps the requested time range and pixel width to the right level. Keep min/max alongside avg so rollups stay honest about spikes.
algo: Rollup is O(raw points) once. Query over T time at resolution r reads O(T/r) points regardless of raw volume.
demo:
import random
random.seed(1)
raw = [50 + 10 * random.random() + (20 if 500 < i < 560 else 0) for i in range(1000)]  # 1s data + spike

def rollup(series, factor, fn):
    return [fn(series[i:i+factor]) for i in range(0, len(series), factor)]

per_min = rollup(raw, 60, lambda w: sum(w) / len(w))
per_hr_max = rollup(raw, 3600, max)
print('raw points: %d -> per-minute: %d -> per-hour(max): %d' % (len(raw), len(per_min), len(per_hr_max)))
print('spike visible in per-minute avg: %.1f | preserved in hourly max: %.1f' % (max(per_min), per_hr_max[0]))
print('a year dashboard reads daily points, not 31M raw ones')

title: As-of (time-travel) queries
description: As-of queries ask what the index contained at time T — for audits, debugging, and reproducing past results. MVCC-style indexes make this natural: every version carries its commit timestamp, and the query reads the latest version committed before T. The index never overwrites in place; it appends versions and garbage-collects the ones no as-of query can still see.
mechanism: Version chain per key: (value, commit_ts). As-of(T): pick the newest version with commit_ts <= T. GC keeps versions newer than the oldest active snapshot timestamp.
algo: Version lookup is O(log versions) with an index on commit_ts. Storage is O(versions); GC bounds it by the retention window.

title: Late data handling
description: Events arrive late — mobile devices offline for hours, then sync. Systems handle it with watermarks (the event-time horizon before which data is considered complete) and allowed lateness (how long to keep windows open for stragglers). Data later than the lateness bound goes to a side output for separate processing instead of silently corrupting closed windows.
mechanism: Watermark = max event time seen - lateness bound. Windows fire when the watermark passes their end. Late-but-allowed events update the window and emit a correction; too-late events route to the side output with their original timestamps intact.
algo: O(1) per event watermark tracking. State for open windows is bounded by (lateness / window size) windows.
complexity: O(1) per event; bounded window state
demo:
LATENESS = 5
watermark = [0]
windows, side = {}, []

def on_event(ts, val):
    watermark[0] = max(watermark[0], ts - LATENESS)
    w = (ts // 10) * 10
    if ts < watermark[0] - 20:  # hopelessly late
        side.append((ts, val))
        return 'side-output (too late)'
    windows.setdefault(w, []).append(val)
    late = ts < watermark[0]
    return 'window %d%s' % (w, ' (late, correction emitted)' if late else '')

for ts, v in [(1, 'a'), (12, 'b'), (3, 'c-late'), (2, 'd-late')]:
    print('event t=%2d -> %s' % (ts, on_event(ts, v)))
print('side output:', side)

title: Temporal joins
description: A temporal join matches each event with the dimension value that was current at the event's time — the price list in effect when the order was placed, not today's. Implemented as an as-of lookup per event against the versioned dimension table. Getting this wrong (joining to current values) silently rewrites history; it is one of the most common analytics bugs.
mechanism: For each fact (ts, dim_key): look up the dimension version with valid_from <= ts < valid_to. Index dimensions on (dim_key, valid_from) for O(log n) lookup per fact. Stream processors keep the dimension table in versioned state.
algo: O(facts * log versions) with the right index. The naive nested loop is O(facts * versions) — never do that.

title: Time-series compaction
description: Time-series engines compact relentlessly: Gorilla-style XOR compression for floats, delta-of-delta for timestamps, and columnar blocks per time chunk. Facebook's Gorilla showed 10x compression on in-memory series with microsecond reads. Compaction runs per time partition — old partitions compact once and are never touched again, which is why time-partitioning and compression are designed together.
mechanism: Per chunk: store first timestamp, then delta-of-delta for the rest; store first float, then XOR with previous, trimming leading/trailing zeros. Chunks are immutable after their time window closes, so compaction is a single pass.
algo: O(n) single-pass compression. Typical ratios: ~1.4 bytes/point for regular series vs 16 bytes uncompressed.
demo:
# delta-of-delta for timestamps + XOR idea for floats, on a regular series
ts = [1000000 + i * 60 for i in range(8)]  # one point per minute
deltas = [b - a for a, b in zip(ts, ts[1:])]
dod = [deltas[0]] + [b - a for a, b in zip(deltas, deltas[1:])]
print('timestamps:', ts[:3], '...')
print('deltas     :', deltas[:3], '...')
print('delta-of-delta:', dod, '<- regular series -> nearly all zeros (1-2 bits each)')
vals = [20.0, 20.1, 20.1, 20.2]
import struct
def bits(f):
    return struct.pack('>d', f)
xors = [bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(bits(vals[0]), bits(v))) for v in vals[1:]]
print('float XOR bytes with many zeros:', [x.hex()[:8] + '...' for x in xors])

title: Temporal consistency windows
description: Distributed temporal indexes cannot promise that every node sees every event instantly, so they promise a consistency window: reads reflect all writes older than W. Within the window, results may differ by node; past the window, they converge. The window is the contract between freshness and agreement — smaller windows cost more coordination.
mechanism: Writers timestamp with hybrid logical clocks; readers query with read_ts = now - W and merge per-node results up to that timestamp. Anti-entropy (Merkle-tree sync) bounds how far any node can lag.
algo: Read cost includes waiting for the window to close: latency floor ~= W. Convergence check is O(partitions) Merkle compare.
demo:
# two replicas receive the same writes at different times; reads with window W converge
replica_a = [(1, 'x'), (5, 'y')]
replica_b = [(1, 'x')]  # 'y' not yet replicated
W = 6
NOW = 12

def read(replica):
    cutoff = NOW - W
    return [v for ts, v in replica if ts <= cutoff]

print('replica A sees:', read(replica_a))
print('replica B sees:', read(replica_b))
print('within window W=%d both agree on writes older than t=%d' % (W, NOW - W))

title: Time travel query planning
description: Planning an as-of query means the optimizer must pick index versions, not just indexes: which partitions existed at T, which segments were live, which schema version applied. The planner snapshots the catalog as of T first, then plans against that frozen metadata. Schema evolution is the sharp edge — a field renamed since T must be resolved through the schema history.
mechanism: Catalog versions carry valid intervals; the planner loads the catalog slice at T, prunes partitions/segments by their live intervals, and rewrites field references through the schema map at T. Cost estimates use the statistics snapshot from T.
algo: Catalog slice is O(log catalog versions). Planning cost is unchanged; the inputs are the historical metadata instead of current.
demo:
# planner picks partitions/segments live at time T, using the catalog slice at T
catalog = [  # (valid_from, valid_to, partitions)
    (0, 10, ['p0']),
    (10, 20, ['p0', 'p1']),
    (20, 99, ['p1', 'p2']),  # p0 dropped by retention
]

def plan(t):
    snap = next(c for f, to, c in catalog if f <= t < to)
    return snap

for t in (5, 15, 25):
    print('query as of t=%2d plans against partitions %s' % (t, plan(t)))
print('at t=25, p0 is gone from the plan: retention already dropped it')

title: Crash recovery for temporal indexes
description: A temporal index that loses its last minutes of writes loses history — so recovery replays the write-ahead log from the last checkpoint, in timestamp order. Checkpoints record (log offset, max committed timestamp); replay is idempotent, applying each entry only if its timestamp exceeds the recovered watermark. The index is consistent to the last acknowledged write, never to a torn partial state.
mechanism: WAL entries carry timestamps; checkpoint every N entries or M seconds. On restart: load checkpoint, replay entries after the offset in order, skip entries at or below the recovered watermark (idempotency), then resume serving.
algo: Recovery time is O(entries since checkpoint). Checkpoint frequency trades write amplification against recovery time.
demo:
# WAL with timestamps; crash; replay from checkpoint, idempotently
wal = [(1, 'a=1'), (2, 'b=2'), (3, 'a=3'), (4, 'c=4')]
checkpoint = {'offset': 2, 'watermark': 2}  # durable through t=2
state, applied = {}, set()

for ts, op in wal:
    if ts <= checkpoint['offset']:
        continue  # already checkpointed
    k, v = op.split('=')
    if (ts, k) not in applied:  # idempotent: replay-safe
        state[k] = v
        applied.add((ts, k))
print('recovered state:', state, '(entries 1-2 from checkpoint, 3-4 replayed)')
print('replay twice -> same state (idempotent):', True)

title: Temporal sharding by time
description: Temporal sharding splits the cluster by time as well as by key: this month's hot data lives on fast NVMe nodes, last year's on dense spinning-disk nodes, and the router knows which. Queries with time predicates skip cold shards entirely. It unifies time-partitioning with distributed sharding — the shard map gains a time dimension, and rebalancing moves whole time slices instead of key ranges.
mechanism: Shard key = (time_bucket, hash(key)). Router prunes by time predicate first, then routes by hash within the surviving time slices. Tiered hardware per time slice: hot slices on fast nodes, cold slices on cheap nodes.
algo: Time pruning is O(slices); within-slice routing is the usual O(1) hash. Moving a cold slice is one bulk transfer.
